newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Delta Three pioneers Internet telephony.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Delta Three pioneers Internet telephony.

text.p: Elie Wurtman, a youthful high-tech entrepreneur in Jerusalem, had a brainstorm two years ago when the first software products for voice communication over the Internet were launched.

Wurtman and partner Jacob Davidson, then in New York, thought how much more convenient it would be for callers if this cheap form of voice communication could be accessed by phone rather than a portable computer.
"We thought the appeal to the mass market of this business would be much wider if it could be accessed from a plain old telephone," said Wurtman.
Enter Delta Three Inc. with Wurtman as chief executive.

Wurtman and Davidson, both U.S.-born, 20-something entrepreneurs, rounded up a team of engineers who pieced together bits of existing software with new technology. The result is an Internet telephony service that allows subscribers to make cheap long-distance calls without a PC.

The system converts standard voice to digital format, breaking down data into multiple packets and routing it over the Internet. At its destination, packets are converted back into analogue format and transferred to the local public telephone network and over to the number dialed.
"A year ago, Delta Three launched its first test product with a service to Israel from Russia that focused on Israel's immigrant community," Wurtman said.
Today, the company has 12 sites in the United States, Europe, South America and Asia.

Calls routed over the Internet amount to savings of about 70 percent for the caller. A call from the United States to Israel, for example, costs just 20 cents a minute 24 hours a day against about 90 cents a minute via a regular service.
The main drawback is a slight delay in transmission compared with regular international calls, which Wurtman equates to the difference between flying economy and business class.
Also, the service takes in only areas covered by Delta Three's network.
Delta Three, based in Jerusalem and New York, is doubling every month the minutes it carries and revenue generated. It expects to continue growing at this rate for the next year.
It has invested more than $1 million and is considering going public on Nasdaq in the next year.
Delta Three is also seeking joint technology ventures and strategic alliances with major telecommunications companies.
By 2001, Internet telephony will account for 20 billion minutes of voice communication a year and Delta Three is well positioned to conquer a large share of the market, according to Wurtman.
"We have a lead time of nine to 12 months because of our early entry into this new arena. By coming in early, we can establish ourselves as one of the major players."

Wurtman and Davidson believe the giant telecommunications companies will not remain indifferent to this phenomenon for long and are more likely to hook up with a company like Delta Three than spend time crafting their own technology.
"It's not worth it for companies like AT&T to develop their own technology. The major companies are too big to move quickly," said Davidson.

Earlier this month, Delta Three took a step toward its goal of becoming a global network. RSL Communications Ltd., an international carrier established by cosmetics heir Ronald Lauder, agreed to acquire a 51 percent stake in Delta Three for $10 million in cash and services.
"With RSL we double the size of our network," Wurtman said.
Seeking to cash in on the global trend of telephony deregulation, RSL is building a traditional switch-based network. It has 13 sites so far with near-term plans for several more.
Eight months ago, RSL gave Delta Three a challenge -- to set up a network to compete in the U.S.-Colombia route. In two weeks, Delta Three was set up in the South American country.
RSL was attracted to Delta for two reasons. "Packet switching is the technology of the future," said Nir Tarlovsky, RSL's vice president of business development.

"It represents a more efficient way of passing traffic than traditional voice. Delta Three is one of the few that actually uses it and is not just testing it," Tarlovsky said in a telephone interview from New York that was carried by Delta Three.
